title: TraceSampler: Making Sampling Errors Predictable and Correctable for Accelerated Generative Sampling

paper.title: TraceSampler: Making Sampling Errors Predictable and Correctable for Accelerated Generative Sampling
paper.abstract: Abstract Accurate sampling from continuous-time generative models can require many model evaluations. Low-step sampling reduces this cost, but coarse updates introduce endpoint errors that can accumulate along the sampling trajectory and degrade generation quality. We introduce TraceSampler, a post-training method that corrects these errors without modifying the pretrained model. Rather than directly optimising the low-step update itself, TraceSampler models its endpoint error as a sample-specific prediction problem. A higher-step reference integration over the same interval provides the supervised target, while a compact representation makes the high-dimensional error predictable from the current sampling trace. This representation combines shared residual structure, directions derived from the trace, and a low-rank remainder, so shallow per-step MLP heads need only predict sample-dependent coefficients. These coefficients drive a two-stage learned residual correction: the first stage predicts the full endpoint residual, while a backbone evaluation at the intermediate state supplies new trace information for predicting the residual that remains; this evaluation is reused by the following step. TraceSampler is evaluated with Rectified Flow on CIFAR-10, SiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, and SD3.5 Medium for text-to-image generation. At 10 steps, it reduces trajectory MSE relative to matched-step Euler by 90.5% on CIFAR-10 and 85.6% on ImageNet-256, while achieving FID scores of 2.692 and 2.189, close to 120-step Heun references of 2.601 and 2.056 with 24 × \times fewer backbone evaluations. On SD3.5 Medium, TraceSampler improves image quality and prompt following; at 10 steps, ImageReward rises from 0.752 to 0.906 while trajectory MSE falls by 70.7%. These gains preserve Euler’s backbone-evaluation budget, add less than 0.4% inference FLOPs, and incur negligible wall-clock overhead, showing that coarse-step sampling error can be made predictable from the sampling trace and efficiently corrected.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Continuous-time generative models sample by numerically integrating a learned ODE from noise to data ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . Fewer steps accelerate generation but require coarser updates whose endpoint errors accumulate along the sampling trajectory and degrade generation quality. The challenge is to approach high-step accuracy with far fewer model evaluations. Existing accelerated samplers reduce few-step error through more accurate numerical updates, optimisation of solver parameters or sampling schedules, and fitted or learned corrections to the sampling trajectory ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . These methods typically improve the update rule itself or fit solver or correction parameters that are determined before inference and shared across samples. While effective, this does not explicitly account for how the error made by a low-step update may differ from one sampling trajectory to another. If these differences are systematic, using the same solver design or fitted correction across samples may leave trajectory-specific error uncorrected. Our hypothesis is that the endpoint error of a low-step update contains systematic structure tied to the current sampling trace, and that a compact representation can make this structure predictable. We introduce TraceSampler , a post-training framework built around this hypothesis. During offline fitting, the deployed low-step update and a higher-step reference integration start from the same state and span the same interval. Their endpoint difference—the coarse-to-reference endpoint residual — defines the step-local error made by the deployed update and, equivalently, the correction required to map its endpoint to the reference endpoint. TraceSampler treats this error as a per-trajectory supervised prediction target; the reference is absent at inference. Because this error is image- or latent-dimensional, predicting it directly is impractical. TraceSampler therefore represents it compactly using shared residual structure, explicit directions derived from the current sampling trace, and a low-rank component for remaining variation. Shallow per-step MLP heads predict only the corresponding sample-dependent coefficients. These coefficients reconstruct trajectory-specific residual estimates. The residual predictor estimates the full endpoint error from information already available in the sampling trace. A frozen-backbone evaluation at the intermediate state then adds new information to the trace, which the residual corrector uses to estimate the remaining error. This evaluation is reused by the following Euler update, preserving the matched backbone-evaluation budget. Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet-256, and SD3.5 Medium, TraceSampler substantially improves low-step sampling. At 10 steps, it reaches FID 2.692 and 2.189 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256, close to 120-step Heun values of 2.601 and 2.056, while reducing trajectory MSE by 90.5% and 85.6% with 24 × 24\times fewer backbone evaluations. On SD3.5 Medium, ImageReward rises from 0.752 to 0.906 while trajectory MSE falls by 70.7%, with improvements in image quality, prompt following, and estimated human preference relative to matched Euler. These gains preserve Euler’s backbone-evaluation budget, add below 0.4% inference FLOPs, and incur negligible measured wall-clock overhead.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work and Positioning
sections.text: Few-step samplers reduce coarse-step error through more accurate numerical updates, offline calibration of solver parameters or sampling schedules, and fitted corrections to the sampling trajectory. Representative approaches include DPM-Solver++ ( Lu et al., 2025 ) and UniPC ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) , which derive numerical update rules; IIA ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , which fits step-wise solver coefficients against finer integrations; and methods such as DC-Solver, DSS, and PAS that optimise compensation, solver/timestep parameters, or low-dimensional corrections ( Zhao et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . TraceSampler differs at the level of what is modelled. Rather than learning or calibrating the sampling rule itself, it retains Euler as the deployed numerical rule and models the realised same-interval endpoint error made by that rule. This error is represented using shared residual structure, stage-specific directions constructed from the current sampling trace, and a low-rank remainder, with the corresponding coefficients predicted separately for each trajectory. TraceSampler therefore performs structured, sample-dependent prediction of the error made by the current update, rather than directly modifying the integration rule or making the deployed correction depend solely on quantities fixed offline and shared across trajectories. Among the closest comparisons, UniPC also has a predictor–corrector structure, but UniP and UniC are numerical state-update formulas, whereas TraceSampler’s residual predictor and residual corrector are learned estimators of error around a fixed Euler update ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) . IIA is closely related through its use of finer integrations offline, but uses them to fit solver coefficients that are subsequently reused across samples, rather than to supervise per-trajectory endpoint-error prediction ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . We therefore focus our empirical comparison on IIA–Euler as a same-base fitted baseline and UniPC as a strong matched-budget few-step solver, isolating the two closest comparisons. The contributions are threefold: (i) casting the realised same-interval endpoint error of each deployed low-step update as a supervised per-trajectory prediction problem; (ii) a structured residual representation combining shared structure, stage-specific trajectory directions, and a low-rank remainder with sample-dependent coefficient prediction; and (iii) a two-stage learned residual correction that uses an intermediate backbone evaluation to refine the remaining error while reusing that evaluation in the following step, thereby preserving the backbone-evaluation budget.

sections.heading: 3.1 Predicting and Correcting Coarse-Step Sampling Error
sections.text: TraceSampler retains an Euler-form coarse update as its low-step backbone and learns the endpoint error made by that update. At step k k , let x k x_{k} be the corrected state at t k t_{k} and v k v_{k} the backbone velocity available to the sampler. The coarse endpoint is x k + 1 base = x k + Δ ​ t k ​ v k x_{k+1}^{\mathrm{base}}=x_{k}+\Delta t_{k}v_{k} , where Δ ​ t k = t k + 1 − t k \Delta t_{k}=t_{k+1}-t_{k} . With few sampling steps, this endpoint can deviate substantially from a higher-step reference over the same interval. During offline fitting, the reference solver starts from the same x k x_{k} and integrates over [ t k , t k + 1 ] [t_{k},t_{k+1}] , giving x k + 1 ref x_{k+1}^{\mathrm{ref}} . Their endpoint difference defines the supervised residual target: r k = x k + 1 ref − x k + 1 base . r_{k}=x_{k+1}^{\mathrm{ref}}-x_{k+1}^{\mathrm{base}}. Thus, r k r_{k} is exactly the correction required to map the deployed coarse endpoint to its reference endpoint. The reference integration is used only to construct offline targets; it is absent at inference. TraceSampler leaves the base update unchanged and learns two residual-estimation stages around it. sections.heading: 3.2 Compact Residual Representation
sections.text: The predictor and corrector residuals have the same dimensionality as the image or latent sampling state, making direct prediction impractical. TraceSampler therefore makes each residual predictable through a compact decomposition into three components: residual error ≈ mean residual + explicit-direction component + low-rank residual component . \text{residual error}\;\approx\;\text{mean residual}+\text{explicit-direction component}+\text{low-rank residual component}. The mean residual captures the correction typically required at a given sampling step. The explicit-direction component captures variation associated with the current sampling trace, while the low-rank residual component captures recurring variation that remains after those directions are accounted for. The coefficient heads therefore need only predict how strongly the explicit directions and low-rank basis vectors contribute for the current sample. The predictor and corrector use the same compact form: r ^ p , k \displaystyle\hat{r}_{p,k} = r ¯ p , k + P k ​ α p , k + D p , k ​ β p , k , \displaystyle=\bar{r}_{p,k}+P_{k}\alpha_{p,k}+D_{p,k}\beta_{p,k}, (1) r ^ c , k \displaystyle\hat{r}_{c,k} = r ¯ c , k + C ~ k ​ α c , k + D c , k ​ β c , k . \displaystyle=\bar{r}_{c,k}+\tilde{C}_{k}\alpha_{c,k}+D_{c,k}\beta_{c,k}. (2) Here, r ¯ s , k \bar{r}_{s,k} is the stage-specific mean residual, P k P_{k} and C ~ k \tilde{C}_{k} are matrices whose columns are the predictor and corrector trajectory directions, respectively, and D s , k D_{s,k} is the fitted low-rank basis. The vectors α s , k \alpha_{s,k} and β s , k \beta_{s,k} are the sample-dependent coefficients for the trajectory directions and low-rank basis, respectively. Each column of P k P_{k} and C ~ k \tilde{C}_{k} has the same dimensionality as the image or latent sampling state. The mean residuals and low-rank bases are fitted offline, while the explicit trajectory directions are constructed from the current sampling path. The coefficient values are sample-dependent: different trajectories at the same sampling step can receive different weights and therefore different corrections.

sections.heading: Predictor directions.
sections.text: The predictor acts before a new backbone evaluation is made, so its explicit directions use only trajectory information already available at the current sampling step. Two directions are constructed: h k = x k − x k − 1 , m k = Δ ​ t k ​ v k − h k . h_{k}=x_{k}-x_{k-1},\qquad m_{k}=\Delta t_{k}v_{k}-h_{k}. The direction h k h_{k} is the displacement made by the previous sampling step and is set to zero on the first step. The direction m k m_{k} measures how the current coarse displacement differs from the previous displacement. Together, they describe the recent sampling motion and how that motion is changing. The directions are normalised before forming the predictor direction matrix P k P_{k} .

sections.heading: 3.3 Sample-Dependent Coefficient Prediction
sections.text: The residual representation defines the available correction components, but their contribution varies across trajectories. Shallow per-step MLP heads therefore predict the corresponding coefficients from trajectory features: ( α p , k , β p , k ) = g p , k ​ ( ϕ p , k ) , ( α c , k , β c , k ) = g c , k ​ ( ϕ c , k ) . (\alpha_{p,k},\beta_{p,k})=g_{p,k}(\phi_{p,k}),\qquad(\alpha_{c,k},\beta_{c,k})=g_{c,k}(\phi_{c,k}). Here, ϕ p , k \phi_{p,k} and ϕ c , k \phi_{c,k} are compact feature vectors containing information available to the predictor and corrector, respectively. Rather than predicting a full image- or latent-dimensional residual, each head predicts only a compact set of sample-dependent coefficients for the structured representation. Each feature vector concatenates trajectory summaries, projections of the current state and recent displacement onto the fitted residual basis, the preceding coefficient-head output from the same stage, and compressed hidden activations from selected blocks of the frozen backbone. The hidden activations are taken from backbone evaluations already required by the sampling chain, so feature construction introduces no additional backbone evaluations. All features are normalised using statistics from the fitting data. Exact feature definitions, targeted blocks, compression operations, and input dimensions are given in Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: 3.4 Offline Fitting
sections.text: Offline fitting estimates the shared mean residuals and low-rank bases, constructs sample-specific coefficient targets, and trains the predictor and corrector heads. Fitting follows the deployed chain rather than treating steps independently: at each non-final step the predictor is fitted and applied before corrector targets are formed, and corrected states are carried forward before fitting the next step. Thus the heads are trained on the chained states encountered at inference. For each deployed correction stage, fitting proceeds in three parts. First, the mean residual is estimated. Second, the weights of the explicit trajectory directions are fitted by least squares. Finally, PCA is applied to the variation that remains, giving the low-rank basis and its coefficient targets. Since the reference residual is known during offline fitting, the coefficient vectors α s , k ( i ) \alpha_{s,k}^{(i)} and β s , k ( i ) \beta_{s,k}^{(i)} can be calculated directly. A separate predictor head is fitted for every sampling step, and a separate corrector head is fitted for every non-final sampling step. Each head is a single-hidden-layer MLP whose final layer is initialised to output the mean coefficient target before training, providing a shared starting point for trajectory-specific refinement. Implementation details are provided in Appendix A.2 . At inference, the reference residual is no longer needed. The saved mean residuals and low-rank bases are loaded, the explicit directions are constructed from the current trajectory, and the coefficient heads predict the sample-dependent coefficients. sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We evaluate TraceSampler with Rectified Flow on CIFAR-10 ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Krizhevsky and Hinton, 2009 ) , SiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256 ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2009 ) , and SD3.5 Medium at 512 × 512 512\times 512 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) . CIFAR-10 supports controlled ablations, ImageNet-256 tests scaling, and SD3.5 evaluates the text-conditioned setting. We report FID, IS ( Heusel et al., 2017 ; Salimans et al., 2016 ) , and trajectory MSE on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256; SD3.5 additionally uses ImageReward (IR), CLIP similarity, GenEval, and HPSv2.1 ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Ghosh et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) . Trajectory MSE measures deviation from the higher-step reference at matched timesteps, with reductions relative to Euler. sections.text: The results first isolate TraceSampler’s design choices on CIFAR-10, then evaluate scaling to ImageNet-256 and transfer to SD3.5 Medium, before examining computational cost.

sections.text: Section 3 leaves the coefficient-head features ϕ s , k \phi_{s,k} abstract; this section specifies exactly what is available to each stage and how those signals are compressed. At sampling step k k , the predictor’s state features use the corrected state x k x_{k} . Its velocity statistics and hidden activations use the backbone evaluation already available at t k t_{k} : the evaluation at x 0 x_{0} for k = 0 k=0 , and the evaluation computed at the preceding intermediate state x ~ k \tilde{x}_{k} for k > 0 k>0 . The corrector uses x ~ k + 1 \tilde{x}_{k+1} together with the newly computed velocity and hidden activations at that state.

sections.heading: Handcrafted trajectory features.
sections.text: The compact trajectory-summary block was selected using held-out permutation importance. Candidate features whose permutation caused negligible degradation for both coefficient heads, including the state spread, state–velocity cosine, and global velocity norm, were removed. The retained features are the per-channel spatial standard deviation of the velocity, the norm of the most recent displacement, and the displacement–velocity cosine. These provide complementary information about update scale and changes in the local trajectory direction. For the handcrafted trajectory summaries, the displacement is defined relative to the state associated with the available backbone velocity. For the predictor, d p , k = { 0 , k = 0 , x ~ k − x k − 1 , k > 0 , d_{p,k}=\begin{cases}0,&k=0,\\ \tilde{x}_{k}-x_{k-1},&k>0,\end{cases} while for the corrector, d c , k = x ~ k + 1 − x k . d_{c,k}=\tilde{x}_{k+1}-x_{k}. For stage s ∈ { p , c } s\in\{p,c\} , the trajectory-summary block is therefore [ std h , w ⁡ ( v ) , ∥ d s , k ∥ 2 , ⟨ d s , k , v ⟩ ∥ d s , k ∥ 2 ​ ∥ v ∥ 2 ] , \left[\operatorname{std}_{h,w}(v),\;\lVert d_{s,k}\rVert_{2},\;\frac{\langle d_{s,k},v\rangle}{\lVert d_{s,k}\rVert_{2}\lVert v\rVert_{2}}\right], where std h , w ⁡ ( v ) \operatorname{std}_{h,w}(v) denotes the vector of per-channel standard deviations over the spatial dimensions h h and w w . For the predictor, v = v k v=v_{k} is the available backbone velocity; for the corrector, v = v k + 1 v=v_{k+1} is evaluated at x ~ k + 1 \tilde{x}_{k+1} .

sections.heading: Targeted backbone blocks.
sections.text: For SiT-XL/2 and SD3.5 Medium, the targeted blocks were selected using layer-informativeness probes. For each candidate block, a ridge readout was fitted from pooled activation statistics to the leading PCA coefficients of the reference–base residual, and predictive performance was measured using held-out R 2 R^{2} across sampling steps. For Rectified Flow, four NCSN++ residual blocks were chosen to span the encoder, bottleneck region, and decoder without collecting activations from the complete U-Net. The exact blocks used for each model are reported in Table 8 .

sections.heading: Activation compression.
sections.text: For SiT-XL/2 and SD3.5 Medium, each targeted activation is projected to 256 dimensions before its token-wise mean and standard deviation are calculated. The common projection dimension keeps the head inputs compact and consistent across blocks with different original widths. Each block-specific projection is fitted from all sampling times of a 4096-sample Euler rollout. Token-mean activations are centred, and their leading 256 right singular vectors define the fixed projection used during coefficient-head fitting and inference.

sections.heading: Feature normalisation.
sections.text: Each feature dimension is standardised separately for every sampling step and correction stage using the mean and standard deviation over all 24,576 collected fitting trajectories. These statistics are calculated before the per-head training–validation split. A feature dimension whose standard deviation is below 10 − 6 10^{-6} is assigned a normalisation scale of one. The stored statistics are reused for validation and inference, where all denominators are additionally clamped below by 10 − 6 10^{-6} .

sections.heading: A.2 Prediction-Head Training
sections.text: A separate predictor head is fitted for every sampling step, and a separate corrector head is fitted for every non-final sampling step. Heads are fitted in sampling order. At each non-final step, the predictor is fitted first and applied to construct the intermediate states used to fit the corrector. The resulting corrected states form the starting states for the following sampling step, so offline fitting follows the same chained state updates used during inference. The training target is the concatenation of the oracle trajectory-direction coefficients and low-rank residual-basis coefficients. The implementation uses an unweighted mean-squared error over all scalar outputs: ℒ s , k = 1 m s , k ​ ‖ g s , k ​ ( ϕ s , k ) − y s , k ‖ 2 2 , \mathcal{L}_{s,k}=\frac{1}{m_{s,k}}\left\|g_{s,k}(\phi_{s,k})-y_{s,k}\right\|_{2}^{2}, where y s , k y_{s,k} is the concatenated oracle coefficient target and m s , k m_{s,k} is its dimension. The coefficient targets are not standardised; only the input features are standardised. Table 9: Prediction-head architecture and training settings. sections.heading: A.3 Residual Decomposition Across Channels
sections.text: A separate residual decomposition is fitted for each sampling step and correction stage using all collected fitting trajectories. After subtracting the stage mean, the explicit-direction coefficients are fitted by the ridge-regularised least-squares system described in Section 3.4 , and PCA is applied to the remaining component η s , k ( i ) \eta_{s,k}^{(i)} . Near-zero directions are treated as zero during normalisation and Gram–Schmidt orthogonalisation for numerical stability. Each explicit trajectory direction spans the full sampling state and therefore uses a single coefficient per sample. Channel-wise decomposition is applied only to the PCA remainder: Rectified Flow uses a single joint pixel-space basis, whereas SiT-XL/2 and SD3.5 Medium use separate PCA bases for each latent channel. Thus, the reported rank K K is the joint PCA rank for Rectified Flow and the rank per latent channel for SiT-XL/2 and SD3.5 Medium. The explicit-direction coefficients and PCA coefficients are then concatenated to form the training target for the coefficient head.

Low-step sampling reduces this cost, but coarse updates introduce endpoint errors that can accumulate along the sampling trajectory and degrade generation quality. We introduce TraceSampler, a post-training method that corrects these errors without modifying the pretrained model. Rather than directly optimising the low-step update itself, TraceSampler models its endpoint error as a sample-specific prediction problem. A higher-step reference integration over the same interval provides the supervised target, while a compact representation makes the high-dimensional error predictable from the current sampling trace. This representation combines shared residual structure, directions derived from the trace, and a low-rank remainder, so shallow per-step MLP heads need only predict sample-dependent coefficients. These coefficients drive a two-stage learned residual correction: the first stage predicts the full endpoint residual, while a backbone evaluation at the intermediate state supplies new trace information for predicting the residual that remains; this evaluation is reused by the following step. TraceSampler is evaluated with Rectified Flow on CIFAR-10, SiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, and SD3.5 Medium for text-to-image generation. At 10 steps, it reduces trajectory MSE relative to matched-step Euler by 90.5% on CIFAR-10 and 85.6% on ImageNet-256, while achieving FID scores of 2.692 and 2.189, close to 120-step Heun references of 2.601 and 2.056 with 24 × \times fewer backbone evaluations. On SD3.5 Medium, TraceSampler improves image quality and prompt following; at 10 steps, ImageReward rises from 0.752 to 0.906 while trajectory MSE falls by 70.7%. These gains preserve Euler’s backbone-evaluation budget, add less than 0.4% inference FLOPs, and incur negligible wall-clock overhead, showing that coarse-step sampling error can be made predictable from the sampling trace and efficiently corrected. Prompt: “Portrait of Leonardo da Vinci as a steampunk cyborg, clockwork automaton with medieval technology.” 1 Introduction Continuous-time generative models sample by numerically integrating a learned ODE from noise to data ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . Fewer steps accelerate generation but require coarser updates whose endpoint errors accumulate along the sampling trajectory and degrade generation quality. The challenge is to approach high-step accuracy with far fewer model evaluations. Existing accelerated samplers reduce few-step error through more accurate numerical updates, optimisation of solver parameters or sampling schedules, and fitted or learned corrections to the sampling trajectory ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . These methods typically improve the update rule itself or fit solver or correction parameters that are determined before inference and shared across samples. While effective, this does not explicitly account for how the error made by a low-step update may differ from one sampling trajectory to another. If these differences are systematic, using the same solver design or fitted correction across samples may leave trajectory-specific error uncorrected. Our hypothesis is that the endpoint error of a low-step update contains systematic structure tied to the current sampling trace, and that a compact representation can make this structure predictable. We introduce TraceSampler , a post-training framework built around this hypothesis. During offline fitting, the deployed low-step update and a higher-step reference integration start from the same state and span the same interval. Their endpoint difference—the coarse-to-reference endpoint residual — defines the step-local error made by the deployed update and, equivalently, the correction required to map its endpoint to the reference endpoint. TraceSampler treats this error as a per-trajectory supervised prediction target; the reference is absent at inference. Because this error is image- or latent-dimensional, predicting it directly is impractical. TraceSampler therefore represents it compactly using shared residual structure, explicit directions derived from the current sampling trace, and a low-rank component for remaining variation. Shallow per-step MLP heads predict only the corresponding sample-dependent coefficients. These coefficients reconstruct trajectory-specific residual estimates. The residual predictor estimates the full endpoint error from information already available in the sampling trace. A frozen-backbone evaluation at the intermediate state then adds new information to the trace, which the residual corrector uses to estimate the remaining error. This evaluation is reused by the following Euler update, preserving the matched backbone-evaluation budget. Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet-256, and SD3.5 Medium, TraceSampler substantially improves low-step sampling. At 10 steps, it reaches FID 2.692 and 2.189 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256, close to 120-step Heun values of 2.601 and 2.056, while reducing trajectory MSE by 90.5% and 85.6% with 24 × 24\times fewer backbone evaluations. On SD3.5 Medium, ImageReward rises from 0.752 to 0.906 while trajectory MSE falls by 70.7%, with improvements in image quality, prompt following, and estimated human preference relative to matched Euler. These gains preserve Euler’s backbone-evaluation budget, add below 0.4% inference FLOPs, and incur negligible measured wall-clock overhead. 2 Related Work and Positioning Few-step samplers reduce coarse-step error through more accurate numerical updates, offline calibration of solver parameters or sampling schedules, and fitted corrections to the sampling trajectory. Representative approaches include DPM-Solver++ ( Lu et al., 2025 ) and UniPC ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) , which derive numerical update rules; IIA ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , which fits step-wise solver coefficients against finer integrations; and methods such as DC-Solver, DSS, and PAS that optimise compensation, solver/timestep parameters, or low-dimensional corrections ( Zhao et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . TraceSampler differs at the level of what is modelled. Rather than learning or calibrating the sampling rule itself, it retains Euler as the deployed numerical rule and models the realised same-interval endpoint error made by that rule. This error is represented using shared residual structure, stage-specific directions constructed from the current sampling trace, and a low-rank remainder, with the corresponding coefficients predicted separately for each trajectory. TraceSampler therefore performs structured, sample-dependent prediction of the error made by the current update, rather than directly modifying the integration rule or making the deployed correction depend solely on quantities fixed offline and shared across trajectories. Among the closest comparisons, UniPC also has a predictor–corrector structure, but UniP and UniC are numerical state-update formulas, whereas TraceSampler’s residual predictor and residual corrector are learned estimators of error around a fixed Euler update ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) . IIA is closely related through its use of finer integrations offline, but uses them to fit solver coefficients that are subsequently reused across samples, rather than to supervise per-trajectory endpoint-error prediction ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . We therefore focus our empirical comparison on IIA–Euler as a same-base fitted baseline and UniPC as a strong matched-budget few-step solver, isolating the two closest comparisons. The contributions are threefold: (i) casting the realised same-interval endpoint error of each deployed low-step update as a supervised per-trajectory prediction problem; (ii) a structured residual representation combining shared structure, stage-specific trajectory directions, and a low-rank remainder with sample-dependent coefficient prediction; and (iii) a two-stage learned residual correction that uses an intermediate backbone evaluation to refine the remaining error while reusing that evaluation in the following step, thereby preserving the backbone-evaluation budget. 3 TraceSampler 3.1 Predicting and Correcting Coarse-Step Sampling Error TraceSampler retains an Euler-form coarse update as its low-step backbone and learns the endpoint error made by that update.
